title: Blind spots — “add search to the docs site”

masthead.headline: Six words asked for search. The site has five versions, a search box already, and nothing that builds an index.
masthead.lede: Nothing here says the request was wrong. It says which decisions the request handed to whoever picks it up, and gives you the chance to make them yourself before somebody guesses.

sections.label: What you asked
sections.title: This is the whole of it.

blocks.text: A short prompt is not a bad prompt. It is a bet that the person reading it shares enough context to fill the gaps the same way you would. This board tests that bet by naming each gap and showing what falls through it.

blocks.caption: The prompt, as sent
blocks.code: Add search to the docs site.

blocks.title: What a reader has to invent to start
blocks.text: Which of five versions results come from, whether the existing command palette grows or a second box appears, what builds and stores the index, what counts as a good result, and who notices when it stops being one. None of those has a default that is obviously right, so each one gets guessed.

sections.label: Overlooked
sections.title: Four things the codebase already decided for you.

points.lead: There is already a search box.
points.text: The command palette opens on ⌘K and searches page titles. A second box means two answers to the same question, and readers will find whichever one is nearer.

points.lead: There are five sites, not one.
points.text: Each published version is its own tree. An index that spans them will confidently return a page the reader's version does not contain.
Whatever is chosen, it adds a build artefact and an owner for it. That cost belongs in the prompt, not in the pull request.

blocks.text: Each card below was found by reading the repository rather than by reasoning about search in general. Tick the ones that change what you were about to ask for.

blocks.label: Which of these change the ask
blocks.ask: Tick every observation that would have altered the prompt if you had known it.

items.title: A search surface already exists and the prompt does not mention it
found: and matches page titles and headings. It has no body text index, which is the part it does not do.
items.impact: Adding a second box gives one question two answers, and the palette is the one readers already reach for. Growing it is a different change from building beside it, and the prompt does not choose.

items.title: The docs are versioned five ways and the prompt names no version
found: is one of them — unreleased, and already the second most visited.
items.impact: One index over all five makes the top hit a page the reader's version does not have. Five indexes make a version switcher part of the search UI. Either is a design; neither is a detail.

items.title: There is no index build step in the pipeline
items.found: The site compiles MDX at deploy and uploads the output. Nothing walks the compiled pages afterwards.
impact: Any answer adds an artefact that has to be built, stored, invalidated and owned. Left unsaid, it lands as

impact.text: a script somebody runs by hand

impact: and stales the first week nobody remembers.

items.title: The three most-run palette queries are navigation, not content
found: The top three terms over ninety days are
— all of them section names in the sidebar.
items.impact: If readers are searching to navigate, full-text search over bodies answers a question they were not asking, and the sidebar is the thing that is failing.

sections.label: What you may mean
sections.title: The same six words, read three defensible ways.

blocks.text: These are not options for how to build it. They are readings of what was asked — different enough that a week of work on one is a week of nothing on the others. Pick the one you meant.

blocks.label: Which reading is yours
blocks.ask: Choose the reading that matches what you had in mind.

choices.value: Grow the palette to search page bodies, current version only
choices.summary: One surface, one version, an index built at deploy from the compiled pages.
pros: Uses the box readers already open, so nothing has to be discovered.
One version means no cross-version result can be wrong.
cons: A reader on an old version searching for a new feature finds nothing and cannot tell why.

choices.value: Full-text search across all five published versions
choices.summary: A dedicated page, its own index per version, and a version selector in the results.
pros: Answers the question a reader on an old version actually has.
Makes the version dimension explicit instead of hiding it.
cons: Five indexes to build, store and invalidate, and a second search surface competing with the palette.
The analytics say navigation, not content, is what people are looking for.

choices.value: Fix navigation; do not add search at all
choices.summary: Treat the top palette terms as a sidebar defect and reorganise around them.
pros: Addresses what the measured queries are asking for.
Adds no index, no artefact and no owner.
cons: Does nothing for a reader who knows the word but not the section.
Reads as a refusal if the person who asked meant search literally.

blocks.recommendation: Grow the palette to search page bodies, current version only

sections.label: Better prompts
sections.title: The same request, written so it cannot be guessed at.

blocks.caption: Left is what was sent. Right is the same intent with the five open decisions closed.

panels.label: As sent
panels.code: Add search to the docs site.

panels.label: As it needed to be
panels.code:
Extend the existing command palette so it matches page body
text, not just titles.

Scope it to the version the reader is currently on. Do not
add a second search box.

Build the index in the docs deploy workflow from the compiled
output, and fail the deploy if the index is missing rather
than shipping a palette that silently finds nothing.

Good enough to ship: searching `retry backoff` returns the
Retries page above the changelog entry that mentions it. Ship
it behind the existing docs flag and read palette terms again
after two weeks.

note: Names the surface, which is the decision the original left open.
also settles that no second box appears.

selections.text: Scope it to the version the reader is currently on.
selections.note: Closes the five-versions problem in one sentence, and closes it the cheap way. A reader who disagrees now has something specific to disagree with.

selections.text: fail the deploy if the index is missing
selections.note: Names the failure mode, not just the artefact. This is the line that stops the index becoming a script somebody runs by hand.

selections.text: searching `retry backoff` returns the Retries page above the changelog entry
note: A single worked example is worth more than an adjective. It is the difference between
and something the implementer can run.
